pages.title: Forty Martyrs of Brazil
pages.text:
The Forty Martyrs of Brazil (also known as the Martyrs of Tazacorte) were a group of forty young Jesuits – 32 Portuguese and 8 Spanish – who were put to death by Huguenot privateers after their ship, bound for Brazil, was captured off the Canary Islands. Taken prisoner, the missionaries were executed on July 15, 1570. Beatified collectively by Pope Pius IX on May 11, 1854, they are commemorated liturgically on July 15 (July 17 in Portugal).


== The event ==
In 1569, Inácio de Azevedo returned to Europe from Brazil to recruit volunteers for the Brazilian mission. On 5 June 1570, he set sail again with 86 missionaries: 70 Jesuits and 16 laymen. As the newly appointed Provincial of Brazil, he was in charge of the group. The flotilla, consisting of three ships led by the merchant vessel Santiago, departed from Lisbon on 5 June. A week later, they reached the island of Madeira, their first port of call. There, the group was warned that the presence of the French Huguenot privateer Jacques de Sores made the surrounding waters dangerous, prompting the flotilla to remain in port for a time.
The captain of the Santiago faced pressure from the merchants financing the voyage and decided to set sail again, despite the danger. However, Azevedo ensured that only volunteers remained on board, while four individuals choose to disembark in Funchal. The expedition was heading for La Palma, the second planned stop in the Canary Islands, where goods were to be delivered and supplies stocked in preparation for the long transatlantic crossing. There were forty Jesuits on board: Azevedo was accompanied by another priest, a deacon, fourteen coadjutor brothers and twenty-three students, most of whom came from the scholasticate in Coimbra.

The ship reached Tazacorte, on the west coast of La Palma, without incident. Upon going ashore, the Jesuits held a religious service in the village church. The ship then set sail for Santa Cruz de La Palma on the east coast, but near the southern cape – off the coast of Fuencaliente – it was intercepted by five privateer vessels. Overwhelmed by the number of attackers, the ship was captured and the passengers taken prisoner. Following the capture of the Santiago, the attackers spared the lives of some members of the crew but Azevedo and his 39 companions were murdered, dismembered and threw into the sea off Tazacorte.
Only one of them, named João Sanches, survived, as one of the privateer ships required his services as a cook. When the privateers docked at La Rochelle, Sanches managed to escape and flee to Portugal, where he revealed the tragic fate of his companions. The news spread rapidly throughout Europe and caused a great stir.


== Canonization ==
Recognized as martyrs for the faith by Gregory XV in 1623 and Benedict XIV in 1742, they were beatified by Pius IX on 11 May 1854. The liturgical commemoration of the forty blessed martyrs takes place on 15 July and 17 July in Portugal. In the calendar of the Society of Jesus, they are grouped with other Jesuit martyrs and commemorated on 19 January. In 1999, forty concrete crosses at the place of martyrdom, about 200 meters off the Fuencaliente Lighthouse were placed on the seabed by the government of the island of La Palma. Adjacent to the old tower, another monument for the Forty Martyrs of Brazil has been erected in October 2014. This monument is a stone cross, with a plate on which the names of the martyrs are engraved.

pages.title: List of early Christian and medieval mosaics
pages.text:
Late Antique, Early Christian, and Medieval mosaics in Europe and the Middle East were created from the 4th to the 15th centuries, mostly in Christian countries.
List includes large and important mosaic pavements and wall coverings from churches and civic buildings (palaces, baths, or villas) and their current or former locations. This list does not include regular geometric floors or small fragments of figurative mosaics in museum collections. The list also includes Islamic buildings whose ornamental mosaics were made by visiting Byzantine masters or were clearly influenced by Byzantine style and technology.
Mosaics are divided into two main types: the older Roman version of opus tessellatum, used primarily for floor mosaics (at least until the 12th century), and, in parallel, the classic Byzantine method with gold smalt, invented by at least the 4th century AD. In the 12th century, the Cosmatesque style emerged in Italy, based on the existing Byzantine technique of inlaid floors (developed from Roman opus sectile).  The Cosmatesque was used for floors and for the decorative ornamentation of walls, tombs, marble pulpits, and so on. The ancient Romans also knew the pietre dure method, but it was rarely used before the Renaissance.
In the first centuries, pagan, antique, geometric, and animalistic themes coexisted in parallel; then Christian ones joined them, eventually displacing them completely.
See also: Late Antique and medieval mosaics in Italy, Early Byzantine mosaics in the Middle East.

Hanyıkığı / Kelenderis, Aydıncık mosaic / Mosaic of Kelenderis — map mosaic (5–6th centuries)
Klarjeti (former Georgia), Akhiza Cathedral (ru) (5th–6th). In 1913, A. Florensky, on a mission from the Caucasus Museum, visited the monastery ruins. According to his information, the altar of one of the churches contained a mosaic image of the Virgin Mary, almost completely destroyed. Florensky reported that a local jeweler named Usta-Gekork had removed the mosaic for sale abroad. Some fragments of the local mosaic are reportedly in museums, but no specific details are available.

=== Georgia ===
near Mtskheta, Kartli Province, Jvari Monastery — the conch was covered in mosaic, but only a fragment remains
Mtskheta, Minor Church of the Holy Cross — old descriptions hold information about presence of mosaics. According to Giorgi Chubinashvili, in 1916, when he visited the church, gold pebbles had survived in the «north corner of the conch, on the face of the arch of the conch»; notches intended for holding the destroyed mosaic composition on the wall were still visible on two stones in the north section of the conch (surface of the rest of the stones in the conch had already been badly damaged and weathered by the time). According to the same account, in 1914, the smalt pebbles scattered in the interior were sent over to the Tbilisi Museum of Historical-Ethnographic Society by the local monk Ilarion (case N1649). The pebbles brought from the church of the Holy Cross are additional material evidence to the fact that the minor church of the Holy Cross in Mtskheta was once ornamented with mosaics.
